Two comparisons for text: has an item starting with any of (`startsWith`), and has no item starting with any of (`notStartsWith`). An item is each part of the text between semicolons, slashes, ampersands or spaces, so a discharge diagnosis written J10.1;R50.9 is two codes, and J10 starts the first. That is how ESSENCE reads a code written ^[;/ ]J10^ in NSSP's syndrome definitions, with the ampersand added for ICD-11's clusters. Evaluated directly, like contains.
A word in double quotes keeps its spaces. " flu " finds stomach flu and not influenza, as NSSP's ^ flu ^ does; without the quotes it was trimmed to flu, which influenza contains.

The mask may be a polygon layer as well as a study area. Both ports are always offered and neither is required on its own; the run refuses two masks, because a point inside one and outside the other has no single answer. A point kept by a layer records WHICH polygon held it, since a layer is many masks and “inside the buffer” loses which one. Built because a buffer around 656 km of border spans 3.59°, which the one-degree scope limit rightly refuses to call a study area, leaving the buffer as a polygon layer that nothing could clip by.

Each polygon replaced by its outer ring, so enclosed gaps become solid. This is isochrone's fillHoles as a step of its own, and it is what Advanced-1 NB03 does: Polygon(new_iso.exterior) at cell 64, the definition that produced the shapefiles NB04 reads. Cell 94 redefines the function to take a convex hull of multipart results and never calls it, which had earlier been mistaken for the operative infill. Takes no UTM zone, unlike the nine widgets that do: the input states the metric CRS its upstream used and this reads it, because a zone asked for twice can be answered twice. The dangerous case governs itself through the port type: donut_geomask, where a hole is the privacy mechanism, emits points and cannot reach a polygons input. See docs/experiments/88-filling-interior-gaps.md.

THE INSPECTOR IS ON THE STANDARD. Settings holds Configure... alone and primary, as every other standard step's does; Retrieve facilities -- or Fetch the registers -- moves to Result, beside what it produces, and is primary until there is something and again when what is held is not what the settings now ask for. The two shared one row before, with the emphasis moving between them by state, so the one thing to do next was whichever the markup had decided. The retrieval is a different kind of act from Configure...: it reaches the network and changes what the step holds, where Configure... only opens a dialog.

The Configure... dialog told the reader to retrieve "under Settings", which is not where the button is. It names Result now, and says to apply the settings first. The matching dialog and the refusal raised when no register has been fetched said the same wrong place and now say the right one.

The Preview never reports a limit shorter than the scan would run. It floored the time share where the scan takes `Math.max(1, floor(bins * maxTimeShare))`, so five days at a tenth read "up to 0 days" of a scan that runs one-day windows.

Says what its keys hide, in the step's sentence of what it did: rows with a blank key, totalled as a group of their own, and names differing only in capitals or spaces, totalled apart; nothing merged or dropped. Found by the table stress tests.

THE TWO VINTAGES ARE COMPARED ON THE YEAR, not as text. It was `numeratorPeriod === denominatorVintage`, so a denominator stated at one precision and a numerator stated at another were reported as two vintages for one year: Rwanda's census of "2022-08" against cases of "2022". Census tables holds four precisions -- 2022, 2022-08, 2022-07-31, 1984-07-01 -- and boundary-source.ts records geoBoundaries returning "2010.0" for one level, so a year reaching a comparison in a form other than four bare digits is the ordinary case. A period no year can be read from keeps the text comparison it had, because somebody who typed the same words in both fields meant them to agree and did agree before this.

THE SIZE OF A DISAGREEMENT, where both periods read as years: "vintages 3 years apart" rather than "different vintages", and `fw:vintageGapYears` in the receipt. One year and forty-one are different findings, and DR Congo's census is of 1984, so a 2025 denominator beside it is forty-one years out and nothing said so. Omitted, in the sentence and the receipt, where no year can be read: an unknown distance is not a distance.

Retired into the two-by-two, which reads events and units at risk from a table and reports the rate ratio. The practitioner, 2026-11-05: 'It should be in the Epi kernel 2x2 widget I think that's what we decided' -- experiment 161, step 6, one substrate and a family of measures over it. This widget read only a Rate step's result, so a table had to pass through a Rate to be compared, and South London was the only workflow that used it. The arithmetic was already shared: both widgets called the kernel's rateRatio, so Snow's 8.401853429780243 (6.84096208049671 to 10.31889085553658) is unchanged to the bit. Retired outright, with no deprecation period, because nobody outside this project uses it (AGENTS.md). A workflow saved with one refuses to open and names it.

The second half of isochrone: walks each street leaving a reached junction as far as the budget left there allows, and buffers the result. Fifth of six primitives an isochrone composition needs, and the one that makes the chain produce a polygon. Restates nothing -- remainingM and travelDirection arrive on the junctions, so the corridor cannot disagree with the traversal that produced them, and junctions from two traversals are refused rather than mixed. Extracting it moved the edge-orientation check and the part-way truncation into src/network-edges.ts, which isochrone now imports too, so the 2 metre endpoint tolerance exists once rather than twice. Takes a UTM zone because buffering in degrees is wrong, which makes nine widgets that each ask for one. See docs/experiments/84-reachable-corridor.md.

A corridor drawn from banded junctions now carries that band's minutes on the polygon, names the feature by it, and says in its notes that a band's corridor contains every shorter band's. Junctions from more than one band in a single corridor are refused, since one polygon cannot stand for two travel times. The minutes attribute already travels into receipts as fw:travelTimeMinutes, which isochrone has always set. Additive: unbanded input behaves as before.

The corridor is the whole route buffered, and the buffer is charged. The walk off the street at the end of a route is now min(bufferM, the budget left at that point), so the corridor is full width while there is time to spare and tapers to nothing where the time runs out, instead of claiming bufferM of ground beyond the budget all the way round its boundary. When the junctions carry the origin’s location, the straight first leg from the site is part of the corridor too. bufferM therefore means the furthest anyone is assumed to walk off a street, not a drawing width. Measured on the John Snow five-minute band: 186,035 m² to 160,415 m². Experiment 114.

The Preview says exactly what it is waiting for, and never asks for something already connected. It was `minutes x speed` -- "That goes up to 800 m along the streets from each site" -- arithmetic on the two numbers just typed, identical whether the network reaches a thousand junctions or none. The budget sentence stays, and what it buys is now counted by `reachableNodes` where the sites and the network can both be read. A downloaded network is held outside the page by reference and read when the workflow runs, so that is said in place rather than asking the reader to connect a network that is already there.

In Show me how, the result pane emptied as soon as a key was found twice, while the sentence beside it said the step "will stop once every row is checked". The practitioner: "There is something wrong with this walkthrough. The result is empty after the last match." Both halves could not be true at once, and the steps that had built Alpha and St. Ann up row by row were made to look as though they had been lying. The renderer was treating two different flags alike: `willStop` is set MID-WALK, where the step is still matching rows, and `stopped` only on the last step, where it has stopped. Mid-walk the rows now stay, because the step really does go on matching them, under the words "None of this will be passed on: the step will stop once every row is checked." Both truths at once, which is what the walkthrough exists to teach: the matching is fine and the outcome is still nothing.

Retired into Table output. No step computed with its points: every widget that measures projects for itself and states its zone, and only a Table could take its output. Showing coordinates in metres is now a choice in Table output's Configure…, with the zone the workflow's coordinates suggest. John Snow's deaths example shows the pumps in metres that way, and a saved workflow opens with each Table it fed reading its source, in the same zone. Retired outright, with no deprecation period, because nobody outside this project uses it (AGENTS.md). docs/audits/reproject-retired.md.
Its satellite-file dialog and sentence moved to sample-raster-ui.ts, unchanged.

THE YEARS BEING STACKED, said in the step's own sentence, and one period per source carried on the stacked table (experiment 230). The population example stacks a 2025 model under a 2022 census and nothing said they were three years apart. Deliberately UNLIKE the unit difference beside it: stacking counts of people under counts of houses is refused, because it is wrong; stacking 2022 under 2025 is said, and the rows are stacked. Silent where no table states a period -- the sentence would otherwise appear on every run and mean only that nobody has said anything -- and where some do, the ones that do not are named, because then the silence is a gap. The WIDEST gap is reported: three tables of 1984, 2022 and 2025 are 41 years apart at their extremes, and "3 years apart" would be true of a pair and false of the stack.
Its Inspector and what opens its Configure… moved out of app.ts into its own module, reached through the kit; nothing it does changed.

Retired into apply_ruleset with the extract-contract ruleset. Experiment 115 read this widget operation by operation on 2026-10-15 and found that NONE OF ITS FIVE OPERATIONS IS ABOUT SEA LEVEL: four are assertions about a table -- its key columns, its unit, its provenance, a column's closed vocabulary -- and one derives a column's distinct values. Every piece of sea-level knowledge it held was in its parameters, and its code was general machinery with that knowledge compiled into it.

Where each operation went, all of it declared data: the six key columns and the two units to inputContract.tableContract; the family pair to its closedVocabulary; the baseline period, the basis kind and the recorded millimetre-to-metre conversion to tableContract.declares; the dataset DOI and the three obligatory citations to basis.evidence, where they resolve; and the distinct site_id values to a knob on the table input, which is P3 -- the constraint lives where the data enters, so a practitioner meets it while they can still fix the file.

Provenance was a refusal wearing a type check: readExtract rejected a plain table because 'the dataset, baseline and citations must be declared first', and the .projection bag it demanded was a token meaning the contract was satisfied. The contract is declared now, pinned by id AND version, which makes 'values are not comparable across dataset versions' true by construction. A workflow saved before today still runs: the assignment step reads the annotated value when it is present.

The practitioner's standard for this, 2026-10-26: 'if another climate model ended up as a ruleset in FW it should be able to use the standard ruleset widget to express and implement its contract' -- and 'no variants'. This widget was the variant, and while it shipped it was a working example teaching the next author to make another one.

Read operation by operation, it held none about sea level: the nearest site and its distance is Measure distance, through the same shared search; keeping only sites the projections file holds is Measure distance's candidate condition or Relate's unmatched rows; the projection at the site is Relate after Select rows. A table port now accepts a distances result, read as a table keyed by point_id, nearest_id and the nearest candidate's own attributes. Retired outright: no outside user.

Retired into the published ruleset compare-level-to-elevation 1.0.0, applied by Apply ruleset (experiment 197). Narrowing to one scenario, family, year and quantile is Select rows; the comparison is two computed values and a margin; what it must not be read as, an inundation model, and the reference surface the elevation must be measured from are the ruleset's declarations. Retired outright: no outside user.

Attaches each site to its nearest network node, measured in metres, and carries how far it moved as a snapDistanceM attribute on the point. Extracted from isochrone, which snaps inside itself and then states in a note that the distance is reported but not charged; on a node of its own that admission is visible and mappable. Third of six primitives an isochrone composition needs, and the first taken from the source end: building backwards stopped because reached edges are truncated mid-street and validateNetwork requires every edge endpoint to be a declared node, so no existing carrier can hold them. Takes a UTM zone to measure a distance, which makes eight widgets that each ask for one. See docs/experiments/82-snap-to-network.md.

A site beyond the snap limit is no longer refused. It is snapped anyway and marked: the point carries offNetworkMetres as well as snapDistanceM, and the activity asserts fw:offNetworkSiteCount and fw:offNetworkSites. Refusing removed exactly the sites furthest from a mapped road, which is where street data is thinnest and where an access question is most often asked. The widget also keeps each site’s own coordinates on the point it moves, as siteLongitude and siteLatitude: it kept only the distance, so nothing downstream could draw or undo the displacement. Experiment 114.

Retired into Map, which takes each polygon layer on its own input, polygons to polygons_6, and collects them for drawing as this widget did: nothing merged, each feature keeping its layer's name, the larger drawn first. The practitioner, 2026-11-13: "This is collect polygon layers widget and I think we can retire it as we can connect polygon layers directly to the Map output." Retired outright, with no deprecation period, because nobody outside this project uses it (AGENTS.md). A saved workflow whose collector feeds only maps opens rewritten, each layer on the map's next polygon input; one feeding any other step is refused and named, since a single polygon input cannot hold several layers. docs/audits/collect-polygon-layers-retired.md.

A boundary acquired below ADM0 can carry its country outline, for context: a province drawn with nothing around it is hard to place. Read from the same geoBoundaries release as the units and as the simplified geometry, 339 KB for DR Congo against 2.4 MB, with its own licence rather than the unit's. It is drawn under everything as a line with no fill, and nothing clips, counts or joins to it.

The widget takes STUDY AREAS as well as polygons, and yields whichever kind it was given. Two adjacent provinces combine into one study area that can be handed to the street network, the facility sources, the clip and the buffer -- which was impossible before, because the only output was a polygons result and nothing that wants an area will take one. The practitioner, 2026-10-22: 'But a study area is a polygon', and 'two study area polygons combined should still be a study area'. No new widget was added: the one whose description already said overlapping and touching areas become one simply recognises areas now.

Combining AREAS does not dissolve a touching border, where combining polygons does. A published outline is an authority's record of where a boundary lies and two authorities describe a shared border differently; welding them would assert a third line that neither drew while citing both. The parts answer every question this application asks of a study area identically. A catchment, by contrast, is this application's own construction, so two that touch are one reachable region and are merged as before.

A PREVIEW, where the section held only Show me how it works. It runs `convexHull` on the points actually connected and says the area inside the outline and how many of them the outline is drawn through -- a hull is decided by its corners, and how few there are says how much of the layer is doing the work.

The Preview draws the polygons shaded by what the step gives each, on Map's scale with its key, and the points that fall in none drawn faint. It also reads the points with their values: it had read the picker's names and locations, so a number to add up, such as DEATHS, was missing from every point in the Preview.

A display choice no longer changes what is computed. "Always show this table wide" wrote `DataTable.wide`, which is PROVENANCE -- it says the file arrived wide, and `isWide` gates on it so Apply ruleset evaluates rules over rebuilt subjects rather than over rows. Keeping the preference turned six rule inputs into three and replaced the measure and value fields with measure-named ones. The preference is `DataTable.shownWide` now; views read either, nothing that computes reads the second. Two more from the same review: a key that varies within a subject is drawn as a column and not only grouped by, so two years of counts for one district no longer appear as two rows neither of which says its year; and the offer to keep a reading is bound on every render, having been bound once while filtering rebuilds the dialog on each keystroke, so the button stayed visible and did nothing.

The coverage port, "Or: Coverage result". Nothing live makes a coverage check: Check spatial coverage retired on 2026-10-21, and a workflow saved with one opens with Keep points inside the area feeding the points port instead.
On the canvas, Table draws what is connected, each with its kind's symbol and the source's name, and one blank port to add another (the buttons-and-ports audit, 2026-11-27).
Configure… previews the table: ten rows, twenty, or all to review, as Results will show them; a polygon table shows its areas from the last run.

A Presentation section in Configure…: title, decimal places, thousands separators, how an absent value is written, shaded rows, notes and source. Every table follows the rules the table standards agree on: numbers right-aligned in equal-width digits, three horizontal rules and none vertical. An absent value is a dash read as "no value" by default.

Retired with Old Naledi, its only example (the practitioner, choosing from two, 2026-11-11). Its arithmetic, distance over a stated speed, is Apply ruleset’s computed column. A saved workflow holding one is refused by name.

Narrows reachable junctions to a shorter travel time, recomputing the budget left at each against the band. The rings of an isochrone map -- 1, 5, 10 and 15 minutes in the case study -- are not four traversals: a cumulative band is a subset, and the notebook's own note says nested thresholds are cumulative rather than disjoint. isochrone recomputes the whole Dijkstra per threshold including the snap, four times over for the Soho example, where one traversal banded four ways gives the same answer. Not a generic attribute filter, and deliberately: reachable_corridor truncates streets by remainingM over lengthM, so keeping a five minute subset of a fifteen minute traversal without recomputing remainingM would leave the longer budget's leftovers in place and draw corridors past the band, silently. The filter and the recomputation have to happen together. Takes no zone and no speed: the speed arrives on the junctions and the traversal's budget is recovered from them.

Each junction kept now carries bandMinutes. reachable_corridor reads it to stamp the band's travel time onto the polygon it draws, so a map can colour by walking time and a chart can label by it, as the case study's outputs do. A layer of lines already drawn reopened showing the whole world. `fitBounds` ran synchronously at mount, when the dialog's panel still had no size, so it fitted the lines into a viewport of 0 x 0 and chose a zoom for that; the `invalidateSize` added the same day corrected the SIZE afterwards and nothing re-fitted. That first fix settled the tiles and not the view, which is why the basemap came back and the lines stayed a world away. The fit now waits for the first moment the container has width and height, and happens ONCE: re-fitting on every resize would throw away wherever the practitioner had panned the moment the panel changed size or went full screen.
